text: Mariam Nabatanzi Babirye, born around 1980 and known as Maama Uganda or Mother Uganda, is a Ugandan woman recognized for giving birth to 44 children, 38 of whom are still alive. As of March 2025, her eldest children are 33 years old and the youngest are eight years old. She first gave birth at age 13 after being forced into marriage the year prior, and by age 36, she had delivered 44 children, including three sets of quadruplets, four sets of triplets, and six sets of twins—totaling 15 births—due to a rare genetic condition causing hyperovulation from enlarged ovaries. In 2019, at age 40, she underwent tubal ligation to prevent further pregnancies after giving birth to her last set of twins via cesarean section, one of whom died in childbirth, marking her most recent child to pass away. Her mother abandoned her and her five brothers shortly after her birth, and at age seven, her stepmother mixed cut glass into the food of her older siblings while she was away, resulting in their deaths. In 1993, at age 12, she was married to a 40-year-old man who was polygamous and physically abusive; her father-in-law provided the family with land to support themselves. At age 13, she gave birth to twins, followed by triplets two years later and quadruplets one and a half years after that. She stated that her father had given birth to 45 children with different women, all in multiple births. After her sixth delivery, she consulted a doctor who advised her to continue having children, stating that stopping would lead to early death, and at age 23, she had given birth to 25 children with a high ovary count. In 2015, her husband abandoned the family, unable to support 42 children, and left her pregnant with twins; he later sold their homestead. She and her children were hosted by her grandmother, and after her grandmother’s death, relatives allowed her to remain in the homestead, though as of April 2023, she still owes a balance on the property before full ownership. Babirye and her household, consisting of sixty-odd individuals including children, grandchildren, and daughters-in-law, live in Kasawo, Mukono district, Central Uganda. They rely heavily on donations for food, beds, and other necessities, and Babirye works part-time as a tailor, herbalist, and hairdresser. Their home complex includes five cement-block houses with corrugated iron roofs and 17 rooms—15 bedrooms and two empty living/dining rooms—nine of which have no beds, six with a total of eight bunk beds (four of which are unusable), and the other four beds accommodate 24 children on mattresses. According to The Uganda Times, Babirye aims to receive UGX 5 million (about US$1,400) to pay off the homestead balance to her grandmother’s relatives to gain full ownership. She also plans to acquire new iron sheets to fix the leaking roofs, 25 new bunk beds, and 66 new mattresses so each person has their own bed, acquire land for farming and animal rearing, and establish a restaurant, bridal salon, and events management service to employ her children and achieve financial security for her dependents.
